section.heading: 10.3. Normal Distributions
Normal Distributions
section.paragraph: In Section 10.2 we saw the useful role played by exponential density functions in many applications. In this section, we look at yet another class of continuous probability distributions, known as normal distributions . The normal distribution is without doubt the most important of all the probability distributions. Many phenomena, such as the heights of people in a given population, the weights of newborn infants, the IQs of college students, and the actual weights of $$16$$ -ounce packages of cereals, have probability distributions that are approximately normal. The normal distribution also provides us with an accurate approximation to the distributions of many random variables associated with random sampling problems.

section.paragraph: The normal curve (and therefore the corresponding normal distribution) is completely determined by its mean $$\mu$$ and standard deviation $$\sigma$$ . In fact, the normal curve has the following characteristics, which are described in terms of these two parameters.

list.item: The curve has a peak at $$x = \mu$$ .
The curve is symmetric with respect to the vertical line $$x = \mu$$ .
The curve always lies above the $$x$$ -axis but approaches the $$x$$ -axis as $$x$$ extends indefinitely in either direction.
The area under the curve is $$1$$ .

For any normal curve, $$68.27\%$$ of the area under the curve lies within $$1$$ standard deviation of the mean (that is, between $$\mu - \sigma$$ and $$\mu + \sigma$$ ), $$95.45\%$$ of the area lies within $$2$$ standard deviations of the mean, and $$99.73\%$$ of the area lies within $$3$$ standard deviations of the mean.

section.paragraph: The mean $$\mu$$ of a normal distribution determines where the center of the curve is located, whereas the standard deviation $$\sigma$$ of a normal distribution determines the peakedness (or flatness) of the curve.

As this discussion reveals, there are infinitely many normal curves corresponding to different choices of the parameters $$\mu$$ and $$\sigma$$ that characterize such curves. Fortunately, any normal curve may be transformed into any other normal curve (as we will see later), so in the study of normal curves, it suffices to single out one such particular curve for special attention. The normal curve with mean $$\mu = 0$$ and standard deviation $$\sigma = 1$$ is called the standard normal curve. The corresponding distribution is called the standard normal distribution. The random variable itself is called the standard normal random variable and is commonly denoted by $$Z$$ .

section.heading: Computations of Probabilities Associated with Normal Distributions
section.paragraph: Areas under the standard normal curve have been extensively computed and tabulated. Appendix C gives the areas of the regions under the standard normal curve to the left of the number $$z$$ ; these areas correspond to probabilities of the form $$P(Z < z)$$ or $$P(Z \leq z)$$ . The next several examples illustrate the use of this table in computations involving the probabilities associated with the standard normal variable.

section.paragraph: We now turn our attention to the computation of probabilities associated with normal distributions whose means and standard deviations are not necessarily equal to $$0$$ and $$1$$ , respectively. In particular, it may be shown that if $$X$$ is a normal random variable with mean $$\mu$$ and standard deviation $$\sigma$$ , then it can be transformed into the standard normal random variable $$Z$$ by means of the substitution

The area of the region under the normal curve (with random variable $$X$$ ) between $$x = a$$ and $$x = b$$ is equal to the area of the region under the standard normal curve between $$z = (a - \mu) \slash \sigma$$ and $$z = (b - \mu) \slash \sigma$$ . In terms of probabilities associated with these distributions, we have

Thus, with the help of Equations (12), (13) and (14), computations of probabilities associated with any normal distribution may be reduced to the computations of areas of regions under the standard normal curve.

section.heading: Applications Involving Normal Random Variables
section.paragraph: Next, we look at some applications involving the normal distribution.

note.source_type: Applied Example 4. Birth Weights of Infants
note.title: Applied Example 4. Birth Weights of Infants
note.heading: Applied Example 4. Birth Weights of Infants
note.paragraph: The medical records of infants delivered at the Kaiser Memorial Hospital show that the infants’ birth weights in pounds are normally distributed with a mean of $$7.4$$ and a standard deviation of $$1.2$$ . Find the probability that an infant selected at random from among those delivered at the hospital weighed more than $$9.2$$ pounds at birth.
note.heading: Solution
note.paragraph: Let $$X$$ be the normal random variable denoting the birth weights of infants delivered at the hospital. Then the probability that an infant selected at random has a birth weight of more than $$9.2$$ pounds is given by $$P(X > 9.2)$$ . To compute $$P(X > 9.2)$$ , we use Equation (14) with $$\mu = 7.4$$ , $$\sigma = 1.2$$ , and $$a = 9.2$$ . We find that

$$\begin{array}{l} {{P\left( {X > 9.2} \right)} = {P\left( {Z > \frac{9.2 - 7.4}{1.2}} \right) {P\left( {X > a} \right) = P\left( {Z > \frac{a - \mu}{\sigma}} \right)}}} \\ {\phantom{P\left( {X > 9.2} \right)} = {P\left( {Z > 1.5} \right)}} \\ {\phantom{P\left( {X > 9.2} \right)} = {P\left( {Z < - 1.5} \right)}} \\ {\phantom{P\left( {X > 9.2} \right)} = .0668} \end{array}$$
Thus, the probability that an infant delivered at the hospital weighs more than $$9.2$$ pounds is $$.0668$$ .

note.title: Applied Example 5. Packaging
note.heading: Applied Example 5. Packaging
note.paragraph: Idaho Natural Produce Corporation ships potatoes to its distributors in bags whose weights are normally distributed with a mean weight of $$50$$ pounds and standard deviation of $$0.5$$ pound. If a bag of potatoes is selected at random from a shipment, what is the probability that it weighs

list.item: more than $$51$$ pounds?
less than $$49$$ pounds?
between $$49$$ and $$51$$ pounds?

note.heading: Solution
note.paragraph: Let $$X$$ denote the weight of a bag of potatoes packed by the company. Then the mean and standard deviation of $$X$$ are $$\mu = 50$$ and $$\sigma = 0.5$$ , respectively.

list.item: The probability that a bag selected at random weighs more than $$51$$ pounds is given by $$\begin{array}{l} {{P\left( {X > 51} \right)} = {P\left( {Z > \frac{51 - 50}{0.5}} \right) {P\left( {X > a} \right) = P\left( {Z > \frac{a - \mu}{\sigma}} \right)}}} \\ {\phantom{P\left( {X > 51} \right)} = {P\left( {Z > 2} \right)}} \\ {\phantom{P\left( {X > 51} \right)} = {P\left( {Z < - 2} \right)}} \\ {\phantom{P\left( {X > 51} \right)} = .0228} \end{array}$$

The probability that a bag selected at random weighs less than $$49$$ pounds is given by $$\begin{array}{l} {{P\left( {X < 49} \right)} = {P\left( {Z < \frac{49 - 50}{0.5}} \right) {P\left( {X < b} \right) = P\left( {Z < \frac{b - \mu}{\sigma}} \right)}}} \\ {\phantom{P\left( {X < 49} \right)} = {P\left( {Z < - 2} \right)}} \\ {\phantom{P\left( {X < 49} \right)} = .0228} \end{array}$$

The probability that a bag selected at random weighs between $$49$$ and $$51$$ pounds is given by $$\begin{array}{l} {{P\left( {49 < X < 51} \right)} = P\left( {\frac{49 - 50}{0.5} < Z < \frac{51 - 50}{0.5}} \right) {P(a < X < b) = P\left( {\frac{a - \mu}{\sigma} < Z < \frac{b - \mu}{\sigma}} \right)}} \\ {\phantom{P\left( {49 < X < 51} \right)} = {P\left( {- 2 < Z < 2} \right)}} \\ {\phantom{P\left( {49 < X < 51} \right)} = {P\left( {Z < 2} \right) - P\left( {Z < - 2} \right)}} \\ {\phantom{P\left( {49 < X < 51} \right)} = {.9772 - .0228}} \\ {\phantom{P\left( {49 < X < 51} \right)} = .9544} \end{array}$$

list.item: Consider the following normal curve with mean μ and standard deviation $$\sigma$$ : Details A symmetric bell shaped curve graphed in the first quadrant of the x y coordinate plane. The curve begins from the x axis, a short distance away from the origin, rises upward to the right, concave up, inflects and then continues to rise upward to the right, now concave down. The curve then reaches a high point and then mirrors its previous path. From its high point, it descends downward to the right, concave down, inflects at the same height as its previous inflection and then descends to the right, now concave up and meets the x axis. A perpendicular is dropped from its high point to meet the x axis at the mark mu such that the curve is symmetric about the perpendicular. To the right side of the mark mu, there is a mark mu + sigma and to the left side of mu, there is a mark mu minus sigma. From both of the marks, two vertical lines rise up till it touches the curve and the area under the curve lies between the marks mu minus sigma and mu + sigma is labeled 68.27%. What is the $$x$$ -coordinate of the peak of the curve? What can you say about the symmetry of the curve? Does the curve always lie above the $$x$$ -axis? What happens to the curve as $$x$$ extends indefinitely to the left or right? What is the value of the area under the curve? Between what values does $$68.27\%$$ of the area under the curve lie?

What is the difference between a normal curve and a standard normal curve? If $$X$$ is a normal random variable with mean $$\mu$$ and standard deviation $$\sigma$$ , write $$P(a < X < b)$$ in terms of the probabilities associated with the standard normal random variable $$Z$$ .
